verdict.headline: Oil cleared $100 and turned an in-line inflation report into a rate-hike week
verdict.label: Headline PPI rose 0.4% with core at 0.2%, under estimate, and the market priced more tightening anyway: WTI settled at $102.48 and Brent at $107.63, hike odds for September 16 reached about 70%, the thirty-year yield rose eight basis points to 5.37% and the S&P 500 fell 0.58% to 7,591.70 for a fourth straight decline
verdict.rationale_short:
August producer prices landed close to consensus and the market sold anyway. Headline PPI rose 0.4% month over month, in line, and core excluding food and energy rose 0.2%, under the 0.3% estimate. On the data alone that argued for less tightening, not more. What moved the session sat underneath the print and after it: final demand goods rose 1.1% against services at 0.1%, with over a third of the goods increase traceable to diesel fuel at 24.1%, and WTI then settled at $102.48, up 6.69%, following the largest attacks on shipping of the six-month Iran conflict.

The repricing came from the barrel, not the data. Traders lifted odds of a quarter-point hike on September 16 to roughly 70% and fully priced an increase by October rather than December. Yields rose six to eight basis points across maturities: the thirty-year added eight to 5.37%, its highest since 2007, clearing August 18's 5.33% high inside a session, and the two-year cleared 4.5% for the first time since 2024. The S&P 500 fell 0.58% to 7,591.70, the Nasdaq 0.65% to 26,081.72 and the Dow 316.56 points to 52,064.10, a fourth straight decline for all three. The VIX rose 8.38% to 17.84.

A supply shock reaches policy differently from a demand one — it raises headline inflation while lowering growth — and the hike odds say the market expects the committee to respond to the first half. The ECB removed the argument that this is a US data quirk: it raised its deposit rate a quarter point to 2.5% the same morning, its second increase in three months, with Lagarde calling it a unanimous "no-brainer" and attributing it to the war's energy shock. Two central banks are now tightening into the same input.

The evidence is not one-directional. Core PPI under estimate is a genuine argument against the market's reaction, and a curve that reprices on one energy settle can give it back on one de-escalation headline: the Iran–Oman temporary transit route, described in early September as in its final stages, would take war premium out of crude without touching the demand underneath it. Gold fell 1.2% into a session of rising war risk, which says the real-rate channel is currently outrunning the haven bid rather than that the risk has receded. This morning's report said the market was pricing the data rather than the input arriving behind it, and that held; it framed the curve's answer as a choice between a front-end and a long-end move, and the answer was both, which is the more inflationary of the two cases it set out.

What would change the picture: a WTI settle back under $100 would say the war premium is deflating and take the input out of the rates move. A core CPI reading at or under consensus on Friday would leave the market priced ahead of its own data with the committee in blackout through September 17. On the long end, a close through 5.44%, the 2007 peak, would put the thirty-year at levels unseen in nineteen years while Treasury's expanded buyback is underneath it; a retreat under 5.33% would say this week's break was the energy spike rather than the fiscal path.
verdict.lede_short: August producer prices came in close to consensus — core at 0.2%, under estimate — and the market priced more tightening anyway, because WTI settled at $102.48 after the largest attacks on shipping of the Iran war. Hike odds for September 16 reached about 70%, the thirty-year rose to 5.37%, its highest since 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 0.58% for a fourth straight decline. Friday's CPI cannot contain September's crude either; a WTI settle back under $100 is what would take the pressure off.

supporting_data.label: Headline PPI rose 0.4% in August and 5.4% over twelve months, with final demand goods up 1.1% against services at 0.1% and over a third of the goods increase traceable to diesel fuel at 24.1% — the inflation in this print is almost entirely the energy channel, which is the one input still rising after the data was collected

WTI settled at $102.48, up $6.43 or 6.69%, and Brent at $107.63, up $6.42, after Iran and the US launched the largest attacks on shipping since their conflict began — the first US settle above $100 this cycle, and a supply event rather than a demand signal

Traders raised the probability of a quarter-point hike on September 16 to about 70% and fully priced an increase by October rather than December — a contested decision became a likely one on a print that was in line, which locates the change in the energy input rather than the data

The thirty-year Treasury yield rose eight basis points to 5.37%, its highest since 2007, while the two-year cleared 4.5% for the first time since 2024 — the whole curve repriced rather than the front end alone, and 5.33%, August 18's prior high, gave way inside a session

The ECB raised its deposit rate a quarter point to 2.5%, its second increase in three months, with Lagarde calling the decision a unanimous no-brainer as the Iran energy shock lifts euro-area inflation — a second central bank tightening into the same barrel, which makes the channel global rather than a US data artifact

Oracle reported Q1 revenue of $19.35 billion against a $19.13 billion consensus, cloud infrastructure revenue up 121% to $7.4 billion and record remaining performance obligations of $664 billion, on $28.5 billion of quarterly capital spending and negative $5.4 billion of free cash flow — the stock closed down 5.38% and rose about 4% after hours, with a backlog funded by borrowing that reprices when the long end does

watchlist_mentions.note: WTI settled at $102.48, up $6.43 or 6.69%, its first settle above $100 this cycle, with Brent at $107.63. The move followed the largest attacks on shipping of the six-month conflict and is a supply event rather than a demand signal, which is why it reached the rates market rather than only the energy sector. $100 is now the floor the week's rate repricing is built on.

December gold fell $53.40 to settle at $4,407.30, down 1.2%, on a day of rising crude and escalating war risk. A metal that sells into a geopolitical supply shock is telling you the real-rate channel is outrunning the haven bid; a hold above $4,400 into Friday's CPI would say the haven demand is still there underneath.

Slipped about 0.9% to near $77,168, losing the $78,000 level it had held for eight sessions. It took no haven bid from the war escalation and traded with the rate-sensitive assets instead, which is the ninth session below $80,000.

Added about 0.3% to near 99.1, tagging 99.12 within half an hour of the PPI release and holding it into the close. This morning's report noted the dollar at a four-month low was not the bid an inflation scare usually produces; that caveat is now spent.

trade_setups.thesis: Crude settled at $102.48, up 6.69%, on the largest attacks on shipping since the conflict began, and Brent at $107.63. The level that acted as resistance all week is now the floor the rates repricing is built on: hike odds moved to roughly 70% on a print whose core reading came in under estimate, which means the barrel rather than the data is carrying the move. The Iran-Oman temporary transit route, described in early September as in its final stages, is the identified catalyst that could remove war premium without touching the demand underneath.
trade_setups.entry: $100 on WTI is the level that defines it; $107.63 is where Brent settled. The route negotiation is the variable that is not on a calendar.
trade_setups.invalidation: A settle back under $100 would say the war premium is deflating and take the energy input out of the rates move.
trade_setups.horizon: Days; tested first by Friday's CPI reaction and the transit-route window

trade_setups.thesis: The long bond added eight basis points to its highest level since 2007, clearing 5.33%, August 18's prior high, inside a single session and doing so while Treasury's expanded buyback program is placing operations of at least $4 billion under the same maturity through November 4. That combination — a mechanical bid underneath and the highest yields in nineteen years above — is the clearest available measure of whether the long end is absorbing supply or being met by it. The 2007 peak is 5.44%.
trade_setups.entry: 5.33% is the level that broke; 5.44% is the 2007 peak above it. The count of completed buyback operations is the second variable.
trade_setups.invalidation: A retreat under 5.33% would say this week's break was the energy spike rather than a repricing of the fiscal path.
trade_setups.horizon: Through November 4, tested first on Friday and at the September 16 decision

trade_setups.asset: August CPI against pricing that already assumes it
trade_setups.thesis: Consensus is 0.4% month over month on headline and 3.4% year over year, with core the line that matters. Like PPI, the print covers August and cannot contain this week's crude. The market has already moved hike odds to roughly 70% for September 16 and fully priced an increase by October, so the data arrives into pricing that assumes its conclusion, with the FOMC in blackout through September 17 and no official able to frame it either way.
trade_setups.entry: Core at or under consensus leaves the market priced ahead of its own data; above it removes the last argument for a hold.
trade_setups.invalidation: A soft core reading that fails to pull hike odds back below 60% would say the pricing is about the oil path rather than the inflation data at all.
